cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Last class, light transferred energy in photon sized packets.
Today we turn that surprise around.
Can something we call a particle show wave behavior?
Yes.
Electrons can produce diffraction patterns, and de Broglie connected their
wavelength to their momentum.
The equation is wavelength equals Planck's constant divided by momentum
magnitude.
Let that idea settle for a moment.
The more momentum a particle carries, the shorter its associated wavelength.
Double the momentum, and the wavelength halves.
This does not mean an electron turns into a little rope that wiggles sideways.
Quantum wave behavior describes the amplitudes used to predict detection
probabilities.
A detector still records individual electron arrivals.
Over many arrivals, the distribution can reveal interference or diffraction.
Even ordinary objects have a de Broglie wavelength in principle, but their
large momenta make it extraordinarily small.
That is why we do not notice diffraction when walking through a doorway.
For our JEE calculations, the most important skill is identifying the correct
momentum, rather than memorizing several unrelated wavelength formulas.
Ask yourself what the question gives: speed, kinetic energy, or an
accelerating
voltage?
Those are different starting points that all lead back to h divided by p.
One more check: two different particles have the same momentum magnitude.
Their wavelengths are equal, even if their masses are different.
Mass matters through momentum, not as an extra factor in the fundamental
relation.
Let's make the comparison questions feel much less mysterious.
For a particle moving well below the speed of light, momentum is mass times
speed.
Substitute that into de Broglie's equation.
Wavelength becomes h divided by m v.
If speed is fixed, doubling mass halves the wavelength.
But do not use that conclusion when the question fixes kinetic energy instead.
Nonrelativistic kinetic energy is p squared divided by twice the mass.
Rearrange it before calculating: momentum is the square root of two m K.
Therefore wavelength is h divided by that square root.
At fixed kinetic energy, wavelength varies inversely with the square root of
mass.
Consider an electron and a proton with the same small kinetic energy.
The proton is about eighteen hundred thirty six times as massive.
Its wavelength is shorter by the square root of eighteen hundred thirty six,
about forty two point eight.
Equivalently, the electron wavelength is about forty two point eight times the
proton wavelength.
Now pause and name the condition before choosing an answer: same speed, same
energy, or same momentum?
That little habit prevents a very common mistake.
If kinetic energy of the same particle becomes four times larger, momentum
doubles and wavelength halves.
These shortcuts assume the nonrelativistic energy formula.
At energies comparable with rest energy, use relativistic momentum instead.
The basic wavelength relation remains h divided by p; the shortcut for p is
what changes.
Now let's connect the wavelength to an experiment.
An electron starts essentially at rest and is accelerated through a potential
difference of magnitude V.
If we neglect energy losses, the electrical energy gained is elementary charge
times V.
That becomes kinetic energy.
First write K equals e V.
Then insert that into the momentum expression.
We get p equals the square root of two m e V.
Finally, wavelength is h divided by that momentum.
For electrons, the constants combine into a convenient numerical relation:
wavelength in nanometers is approximately one point two two seven divided by
the square root of V in volts.
Please keep those units attached to the shortcut.
At one hundred volts, the square root is ten, so the wavelength is zero point
one two two seven nanometers.
That is also one point two two seven angstroms.
Your turn.
What happens at four hundred volts?
The voltage became four times larger, not twice.
Take a moment.
The wavelength halves, giving zero point zero six one three five nanometers.
The electron gains one hundred electron volts in the first case and four
hundred electron volts in the second.
These are tiny compared with its rest energy of roughly five hundred eleven
kilo electron volts, so the nonrelativistic approximation is excellent here.
If initial kinetic energy is not negligible, add it to the energy gained.
Do not blindly set total kinetic energy equal to e V.
Here is a useful comparison that catches a sneaky substitution error.
A photon and an electron can have the same numerical energy, but that does not
give them the same momentum.
A photon has zero rest mass, yet it carries momentum.
Its momentum is energy divided by c.
Therefore its wavelength is h c divided by energy.
Do not try to calculate photon momentum as rest mass times speed; that would
incorrectly give zero.
An ordinary low energy electron instead has momentum given by the square root
of two m K.
Let's compare a one hundred electron volt photon with an electron having one
hundred electron volts of kinetic energy.
Using h c approximately twelve hundred forty electron volt nanometers, the
photon wavelength is twelve point four nanometers.
For the electron, our voltage shortcut from the previous chapter gives zero
point one two two seven nanometers.
The photon wavelength is about a hundred times longer in this particular
comparison.
It is not a universal fixed ratio; the two energy dependencies are different.
Doubling photon energy halves its wavelength.
Quadrupling a nonrelativistic electron's kinetic energy halves its wavelength.
Before solving a mixed question, write the particle name next to the energy
symbol.
For a massive particle, distinguish kinetic energy from total relativistic
energy.
For a photon, E is its energy, with no rest energy subtraction.
The common rule is still wavelength equals h over p.
The physical model decides how energy gives us p.
An equation becomes much more convincing when nature agrees with it.
Davisson and Germer observed a directional diffraction pattern when electrons
scattered from a crystal.
Regularly spaced crystal planes provide path differences between contributions
from different layers.
In a simple Bragg geometry, constructive interference requires twice the plane
spacing times sine theta to equal an integer number of wavelengths.
Here theta is the angle the incident direction makes with the planes, not
automatically the angle between incident and detected beams.
The drawing is an idealized geometry, not a detailed reconstruction of their
apparatus.
Suppose the plane spacing is zero point two nanometers and the wavelength is
also zero point two nanometers.
For first order, the equation says two times zero point two times sine theta
equals zero point two.
Sine theta is one half, so theta is thirty degrees.
Pause before using an inverse sine in another example.
Its argument must be between minus one and one; an impossible value means that
diffraction order cannot occur in that geometry.
Individual electrons still arrive as localized events.
The repeated detection pattern reveals the wave prediction.
For JEE, the central syllabus result is the de Broglie relation, and this
experiment explains why we take it seriously.
Finish every numerical problem by checking the stated condition, choosing
momentum correctly, and converting the final wavelength units.
Same momentum means same wavelength.
That is the anchor to come back to.
